source.title: From Noise to Narrative: Tracing the Origins of Hallucinations in Transformers
source.authors: Praneet Suresh; Jack Stanley; Sonia Joseph; Luca Scimeca; D. Bzdok

record.tranche_reason: Extends analysis of recoverable sparse features to pretrained vision and language transformers using SAE-based measurements and interventions; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and discusses linear representations, but does not test feature competition for capacity, a sparsity-dependent superposition transition, or feature directions versus dimensions. Included results concern SAE feature recovery, stability, and feature interventions. Hallucination-prediction benchmark comparisons and other results that do not measure these features are not cataloged.
record.test_reason: The study mainly uses SAEs as a tool to study hallucination. Two incidental results still bear on the claim. Noise-trained CLIP SAEs yield ImageNet-interpretable, partly steerable concepts (V4). SAEs trained with different seeds share only 14–35% of sampled concepts (V5 stability). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that pretrained transformers impose coherent, steerable concepts on noise or shuffled inputs. They find concept usage expands as input structure degrades, mainly in middle layers. They report that input-prompt SAE concept activations predict hallucination, and that suppressing key concepts lowers hallucination scores. They caution that SAEs are not perfect oracles.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders to identify and evaluate concepts in pretrained transformers, with input perturbations, feature steering, and feature suppression; it does not use the Toy Models of Superposition toy-network setup or test its geometric transition.
record.method_sensitivity: Input perturbation level and modality affect SAE L0; concept overlap varies by transformer layer, with lower overlap in middle layers.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE L0 (number of active features) rises under input shuffling, peaking in middle layers. Shown for CLIP layer 6 (+38) and Pythia layer 9 (+81).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Degraded inputs recruit more SAE features in middle transformer layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Suppressing the 10 PLS-selected layer-11 Gemma SAE features lowers mean HHEM hallucination score from 0.91 to 0.72 on the most hallucinated quartile.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-prompt SAE features predict and causally influence summary hallucination.

record.problems: The paper states that SAEs are not perfect oracles for interpretability and that generalization to frontier models with 10-100+ billion parameters remains unknown. Some layer-wise concept percentages are presented in figures without exact values in the text. The stability analysis compares a sampled subset of SAE concepts and does not test completeness or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results left out. The tables comparing hallucination-detection methods on TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, and CoQA were excluded because their scores evaluate prediction methods rather than the superposition-related properties or recoverability of SAE features.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry of feature directions.
No test of capacity competition or importance-based allocation.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across neurons. No SAE-recovery test on natural-input LLM features beyond using pretrained Gemma SAEs as a tool.
Completeness and canonicality not tested directly. Stability tested only for noise-trained CLIP SAEs across seeds.
Assumes 1-D linear directions; no test against multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: SAE reconstruction quality and alive-feature rates, which bear on how complete the dictionaries are. ViT SAEs: explained variance 0.99. Pythia SAEs: explained variance 0.70–0.92 by layer, alive features down to 22% at layer 12.
Layer-wise percentages of interpretable and steerable noise-SAE concepts.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mostly a hallucination paper that uses SAEs as a tool. Its relevance to superposition is incidental. The seed-overlap result (Appendix C) is the most direct evidence, on V5 stability. The authors read it as a 'consistent core' and evidence of 'conceptual wandering', but the overlap numbers show most features do not recur. The hallucination-detection benchmark tables were rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No test of more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
No test of polysemantic neurons as a consequence of limited capacity or of importance-based allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity mechanisms causing polysemantic neurons.
Does not measure features spread across neurons or establish how broadly the findings generalize beyond the tested models, datasets, and SAE setups.
Tests overlap of concepts across SAE runs, but not completeness or whether SAE features are canonical units of the model.
Uses SAE decoder directions but does not test whether the underlying features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B/32
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on LAION dataset with 1.4 billion image-text pairs
rows.operation_detail: Measured semantic purity of concepts from layer-wise SAEs trained on Gaussian-noise activations.
rows.measure: Semantic purity of SAE concepts; interpreted as coherent semantic concepts at purity at least 0.75.
rows.value: The authors report many high-purity features, each corresponding to a coherent high-level concept; exact percentages not stated.
rows.note: The paper says the concepts were sampled from noise-trained SAEs and evaluated using ImageNet images. Figure 3 reports layer-wise percentages, but exact values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The value is only verbal; Figure 3 gives percentages not reproduced in the text. The SAEs were trained on Gaussian-noise activations, not natural inputs, so this is indirect evidence on recoverable features.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B/32
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on LAION dataset with 1.4 billion image-text pairs
rows.operation_detail: Added a scaled SAE decoder direction to residual-stream activations for neutral images.

conditions.value: 32 images per feature for the stated steerability criterion

rows.measure: Whether the model's top-1 label switches to the feature's majority label after feature-direction addition.
rows.baseline: Neutral images originally do not activate the feature; original label-switch rate not stated.
rows.value: A non-negligible number of highly interpretable concepts were steerable, particularly in early and middle layers; exact count not stated. The stated criterion was 32 out of 32 images switching.
rows.note: Steerability shows that some SAE-recovered concepts can influence model outputs; the paper does not provide exact layer-wise counts in the text.
rows.check: The text says a 'non-negligible number' of concepts are steerable, a subset of the interpretable ones. Counts are figure-only. This shows causal relevance for some features only.

rows.subject: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean SAE L0 for natural versus 28x28 patch-shuffled images.
rows.measure: Mean number of non-zero SAE concepts (L0).
rows.note: The main text describes this as about 38 additional concepts on average for the smallest patch size.
rows.check: An L0 rise under patch shuffling measures concept-count expansion under perturbation. It does not test whether sparse features are recoverable or spread across neurons.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m-deduped
rows.stage_stated: trained on 300 billion tokens from the Pile
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean SAE L0 for natural versus single-word-shuffled text.
rows.measure: Mean number of non-zero SAE concepts (L0).
rows.note: The main text reports 81 extra concepts triggered on average at the peak; the table gives the means shown here.
rows.check: Same as r3: the L0 change under word shuffling does not bear on any version. Values match Table 7 (difference about 81).

rows.subject: Gemma 2B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Set the 10 highest-VIP layer-11 SAE concept activations to zero and replaced the residual-stream activations with decoded, modified activations during generation.
rows.measure: Mean HHEM-2.1 hallucination score for generated summaries.
rows.note: This is an induced intervention, not a measure of the natural prevalence of hallucinations. It shows that selected SAE features can affect generated output.
rows.check: A hallucination-score change after suppressing PLS-selected features is an intervention outcome of the authors' method. It is not a measure of superposition or feature recoverability.

rows.subject: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Compared concepts from two Gaussian-noise-trained SAE sets with different initialization seeds using Jaccard overlap.
rows.measure: Jaccard index of concepts shared between SAE sets.
rows.note: The authors describe a consistent core of concepts; this measures run-to-run overlap, not completeness or canonicality.
rows.check: 35% Jaccard overlap across seeds in the first three layers, on a randomly sampled feature subset. The matching criterion for 'same concept' is not specified.

rows.subject: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Compared concepts from two Gaussian-noise-trained SAE sets with different initialization seeds using Jaccard overlap.
rows.measure: Jaccard index of concepts shared between SAE sets.
rows.note: The paper describes overlap as dropping sharply in these layers and interprets this as a broader, less consistent concept space.
rows.check: 14% overlap at layers 5–6. Most sampled concepts are not reproduced across seeds.

rows.subject: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Compared concepts from two Gaussian-noise-trained SAE sets with different initialization seeds using Jaccard overlap.
rows.measure: Jaccard index of concepts shared between SAE sets.
rows.note: The authors report a rebound to a more stable set of high-level features; completeness and canonicality are not measured.
rows.check: 25% overlap in deeper layers. This is still well below a stable dictionary.

relationships.condition: Noise-trained layer-wise SAEs on OpenCLIP ViT-B/32, probed with ImageNet validation images
relationships.reason: Many sampled SAE directions have semantic purity ≥0.75, and some steer top-1 labels on 32/32 neutral images (r1, r2). Exact rates are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Many sampled SAE directions had semantic purity of at least 0.75, and some steered the top-1 label on 32 of 32 neutral images.

relationships.condition: Noise-trained CLIP ViT-B/32 SAEs, two seeds, randomly sampled feature subset
relationships.reason: Only 35% (early), 14% (middle) and 25% (late) of sampled concepts recur across seeds. SAE features are therefore far from stable units (r6–r8).
relationships.display_finding: Only 35% of sampled concepts recurred across seeds in early layers, 14% in middle layers and 25% in late layers.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested SAE setups on CLIP-ViT-B/32, Pythia-160m-deduped, and Gemma 2B-IT
reader_labels.reason: SAEs yielded coherent semantic concepts, increased numbers of active concepts under input scrambling, and concepts whose targeted intervention changed model outputs (r1-r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Noise-trained CLIP-ViT-B/32 SAEs compared across initialization seeds
reader_labels.reason: Concept overlap varies by layer, falling to 14% at layers 5-6; the measurements support some recurring concepts but do not establish complete or canonical units (r6-r8).
